title: The Storm of the Century

jokes.text: Well, I, for one, would like to meet this Jackie Denardo and see if her breasts are as staggering in person.
jokes.setup: The TV news anchor is delivering an urgent, serious hurricane warning about a catastrophic storm threatening Philadelphia.
jokes.punchline: Dennis pivots from life-threatening weather coverage to evaluating the anchor's breasts as the primary takeaway.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny cold open pivot — the gap between the gravity of the news and Dennis's completely unrelated preoccupation is well-timed. 'Staggering in person' is a funny word choice. Character-specific to Dennis's preening narcissism and objectifying nature. Sets up the Jackie Denardo running thread efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, I, for one, would like to meet this Jackie Denardo and see if her breasts are as staggering in person.

jokes.text: Guys, maybe we should get a 3-D TV. The breasts are only going to keep getting bigger, and we need the latest technology to keep up.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just noted the anchor's breasts. Charlie treats this as a rational, forward-thinking consumer electronics problem.
jokes.punchline: 'We need the latest technology to keep up' — the deadpan logic that breast size inflation is a technological arms race.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Charlie's earnest, practical framing of a completely absurd premise. 'Keep up' implies a technological race against nature that is perfectly Charlie-brained. Good economy; every word earns its place. Sets up the 3-D TV callback that pays off beautifully at the episode's climax.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Guys, maybe we should get a 3-D TV. The breasts are only going to keep getting bigger, and we need the latest technology to keep up.

jokes.text: Are you guys kidding me? You're focused on boobies at a time when a massive storm is about to hit Philadelphia?
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie have enthusiastically pivoted from hurricane coverage to discussing breast size and 3-D TV.
jokes.punchline: Dee's indignant straight-man call-out using the word 'boobies' — which slightly undercuts her moral authority.
jokes.explanation: Functional straight-man beat. Dee's use of 'boobies' rather than a more outraged word is a small grace note. This is necessary scaffolding rather than a great joke on its own — it establishes the dynamic and allows the guys' response to land.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, she's talking about it and, you know, we're sort of listening and we're enjoying her breasts. Just let us have this. The breasts make you care about the weather in a really good way

jokes.text: She's talking about it, and, you know, we're sort of listening and we're enjoying her breasts. Just let us have this.
jokes.setup: Dee has called them out for being distracted by the anchor's body during a hurricane warning.
jokes.punchline: 'Just let us have this' — a plaintive, almost reasonable request to be allowed to simultaneously panic-watch the news and ogle.
jokes.explanation: 'Just let us have this' is a legitimately quotable line. The word 'sort of' preceding 'listening' is a nice hedge that acknowledges they're doing neither thing well. The phrase has the rhythm and resignation of a genuinely defeated person, which makes it funnier. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Amigos, tenemos... Ho! Whoo! Cha, cha, cha. Oh, man, it's internacional. It's on every channel. These are the breasts we should focus on.

jokes.text: The breasts make you care about the weather in a really good way.
jokes.setup: Dee is pushing back on their breast fixation during a hurricane emergency.
jokes.punchline: Dennis offers a sincere, almost civic defense: the breasts are actually improving weather literacy.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The construction is perfect: it frames objectification as a public service, delivered with total sincerity. 'In a really good way' is a killer qualifier — the implied contrast ('as opposed to a bad way') is absurd. Very Dennis: self-serving rationalization dressed up as wisdom. Highly quotable and extremely economical.

dialogue.line: What are you wearing?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, I got all riled up by the weather report and ain't a drop of rain out there, so I put this old trash bag on to keep myself protected.

jokes.text: Channel 5 News cuts to a Spanish-language broadcast with a Latina anchor — 'Cha-cha-cha! ¡Rica!' — and the guys immediately fixate on her too.
jokes.setup: Mac concedes that maybe they're too focused on the first anchor's breasts and suggests switching to Channel 5.
jokes.punchline: Channel 5 also has an attractive anchor; the guys' enthusiasm resets instantly, now framed as 'it's internacional!' — their fixation travels across language and culture.
jokes.explanation: Solid escalation gag: the apparent self-correction ('maybe we're too focused') is immediately revealed to be a redirect to more of the same. 'It's internacional!' is a funny coinage. The structure is clean — setup the pivot, subvert it. Not exceptional but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That was the Mayans, dude.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Mayans, Mexicans-- what's the difference?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: One difference is that the Mayans are extinct.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, the Mexicans killed the Mayans.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, the Spaniards banged the Mayans, turned 'em into Mexicans.

jokes.text: These are the breasts we should focus on.
jokes.setup: Mac appeared to be redirecting them away from breast-ogling. Channel 5 reveals a new attractive anchor.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately declares the new anchor's breasts the correct object of focus, with the word 'should' implying this is the rational, correct conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Very economical — five words that do a lot of work. The 'should' transforms the sentence from lust into a proclamation of duty. Works as a quick button on the channel-switch gag.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We got to stop pussydicking around here, okay? It's time to get in the bunker.

jokes.text: Frank enters wearing a DIY trash bag poncho, announces there's not a drop of rain outside.
jokes.setup: The gang has been watching alarming hurricane coverage and working themselves into a frenzy.
jokes.punchline: Frank barrels in wearing a garbage bag as rain protection to report that it isn't raining at all — the preparation was entirely unnecessary, and the outfit is absurd.
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank entrance: physical absurdity (trash bag poncho) combined with the deflating information that his preparation was for nothing. The visual and the news arrive simultaneously, which is tight construction. Very Frank — impulsive, self-sufficient, undignified.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, we, uh, we converted this old storage closet into a place where we could ride out Y2K.

jokes.text: So I put this old trash bag on to keep myself protected. / You did it for nothing, huh?
jokes.setup: Frank is wearing a trash bag in anticipation of rain that hasn't materialized.
jokes.punchline: Mac's flat 'You did it for nothing, huh?' — accepting the absurdity without judgment.
jokes.explanation: Mac's response is the joke — the complete lack of surprise or commentary on the trash bag outfit, just a mild acknowledgment of wasted effort. Functional comic beat that relies on understatement and the show's established 'nothing fazes anyone' dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, robopocalypse-- machines communicating with each other and conspiring to destroy the human race.

jokes.text: Dude, maybe the Mexicans were right. / That was the Mayans, dude. / Mayans, Mexicans... What's the difference?
jokes.setup: The storm news is escalating and Mac says it might be the end of days. Charlie invokes 2012 prophecy attributed to 'the Mexicans.'
jokes.punchline: Mac corrects him (Mayans), and Charlie responds with 'Mayans, Mexicans... What's the difference?' — genuine ignorance delivered as a dismissive rhetorical question.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie stupidity — not malicious, just profoundly ignorant. The joke is that he's asking 'what's the difference?' as though it's an impossible pedantry rather than basic history. Sets up an escalating exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And why is there a condom wrapper on the floor?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Uh, you've probably been banging in the bunker, right?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Guilty.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I've been watching him bang in here.

jokes.text: One difference is that the Mayans are extinct. / Yeah. The Mexicans killed the Mayans. / No, the Spaniards banged the Mayans, turned 'em into Mexicans.
jokes.setup: Mac tries to correct Charlie's conflation of Mayans and Mexicans by pointing out the Mayans are extinct.
jokes.punchline: Charlie accepts the extinction but credits Mexicans for it; Mac then provides a crudely reductive but partially accurate account of Spanish colonization as 'the Spaniards banged the Mayans, turned 'em into Mexicans.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best exchanges. The escalation is perfect: Charlie's wrong answer ('Mexicans killed the Mayans') is a logical failure mode from his initial confusion, and Mac's correction — 'the Spaniards banged the Mayans, turned 'em into Mexicans' — is simultaneously crude, funny, and not entirely historically inaccurate (mestizaje). The word 'banged' doing all the historical heavy lifting is inspired. Both characters stay perfectly in-voice.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't rape girls, come on.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I don't eat that many pickled eggs, but...

jokes.text: Yeah, we converted this old storage closet into a place where we could ride out Y2K.
jokes.setup: Frank announces the gang should get in 'the bunker.'
jokes.punchline: The bunker is revealed to be a converted storage closet built specifically for Y2K — a panic that never materialized, making the preparation both touching and pathetic.
jokes.explanation: Good worldbuilding joke that retroactively establishes the gang's history of overreacting to media hysteria. The Y2K bunker is funny because it's specific, pathetic, and entirely believable for these characters. Sets up the reveal that it's been raided.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And they have left, they have left now. I'm only still here 'cause I'm not as quick as them.

jokes.text: Dee got us all worked up about the computers taking over mankind, and then she had us build this bunker. / Yeah, robopocalypse... machines communicating with each other and conspiring to destroy the human race.
jokes.setup: Frank reminisces about why they built the Y2K bunker.
jokes.punchline: Dee apparently was the alarmist who convinced them to build a doomsday bunker over Y2K, and her theory was 'robopocalypse' — machines conspiring against humanity. She then half-defends it.
jokes.explanation: Funny inversion: Dee, the designated voice of reason in this episode, was apparently the most hysterical alarmist in the past. 'Robopocalypse' is a great word. Sets up her recurring insistence about machine dependency paying off during the credit card machine failure later.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Is that a pickled egg?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, it's an egg I brought from home.

jokes.text: Is it nonsense? Or is it nonsense that we rely solely on computers to run every aspect of our lives?
jokes.setup: Frank calls Dee's robopocalypse theory 'complete nonsense.'
jokes.punchline: Dee's rhetorical self-defense is structurally identical to her accusation — she's essentially saying 'Is it nonsense? Or is it... also the same nonsense?' — which inadvertently proves Frank's point while she thinks she's winning.
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment — Dee's argument collapses on itself. The 'is it nonsense? Or is it...' construction is a rhetorical cliché that the show deploys here to show Dee getting flustered. Also sets up the credit card machine payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Hey, you know what I was thinking? In addition to supplies, might be nice to grab some girls, you know, get them back to the bar. This Jackie Denardo chick-- she's, uh, sparked another storm inside me if you know what I mean.

jokes.text: We raided the bunker directly after Y2K. / Well, now it's empty.
jokes.setup: Frank excitedly shows them the Y2K bunker as their hurricane refuge.
jokes.punchline: The bunker was completely raided immediately after Y2K ended — meaning the first thing they did after the apocalypse didn't happen was eat all the survival food.
jokes.explanation: The 'directly after Y2K' timing detail is what makes this land — not eventually, not over months, but immediately. The word 'directly' implies they were popping sardine cans at 12:01 AM January 1, 2000. Good character-consistent behavior: these people have no impulse control.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, and we could use 'em to repopulate the planet or something.

jokes.text: And why is there a condom wrapper on the floor? / You've probably been banging in the bunker, right? / Guilty. I've been watching him bang in here.
jokes.setup: The gang discovers the supposedly emergency-ready bunker is empty and apparently has been used for other purposes.
jokes.punchline: Frank guesses someone has been having sex in there; Charlie confirms not only that Frank is right but that Charlie has been watching — a deeply unsettling admission delivered with complete casualness.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly escalated three-step revelation: (1) condom wrapper discovered, (2) Frank guesses someone was having sex, (3) Charlie casually admits he was watching. The third step is the unexpected escalation that makes this land hard. Charlie's voyeurism is treated as completely normal by him, which is the core joke. Very character-specific: only Charlie could deliver 'I've been watching him bang in here' as a breezy admission. The 'Guilty' from Frank before Charlie's escalation is also a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Okay, I'd at least like to find one, like, Mexican or Mayan or something for predictions.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, but get some batteries, though. You be the battery guy and I'll be the, the chicks and tits guy.

jokes.text: Yeah, he was probably down here with Mac, watching you rape girls, and eating pickled eggs. / I don't rape girls. Come on. / Yeah, and I don't eat that many pickled eggs.
jokes.setup: Dee speculates on what the bunker has been used for.
jokes.punchline: Frank's defense prioritizes denying rape, which is a low bar; Charlie's defense prioritizes the pickled egg quantity — his concern is about the food characterization, not the rape characterization.
jokes.explanation: Dark and very funny. The genius is in the inversion of priorities: Frank denies rape as though that's the reasonable clarification to make; Charlie's objection is entirely about how many pickled eggs he ate — the rape accusation goes unchallenged by him. Both responses are perfectly character-specific. Charlie's egg quantity caveat ('that many') implies he ate some, just not an unreasonable amount. This is high-craft Always Sunny dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: When it's white people, it's survival, and when it's black people, it's looting.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: No, Frank, it's because the white people are stealing bread, and the black people are stealing speakers.

jokes.text: But, well, you know what? Let's stock up on some more pickled eggs down here though.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just been accused of watching sex acts and eating pickled eggs in the bunker.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate response is to plan to restock the pickled eggs — no acknowledgment of the other issues, just practical food planning.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie beat — his fixation is entirely on the eggs, not on the other implications of the previous exchange. The 'you know what?' as a conversational pivot is very true to how the character speaks. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: How do you know the blacks don't have bread in those speakers?

jokes.text: It's in our minds, you know. And she's in my mind. Let's go there.
jokes.setup: Frank questions whether going to the All American Home Center is falling for media manipulation.
jokes.punchline: Dennis conflates the store being 'in their minds' from the news broadcast with the news anchor being 'in his mind' — using the same language for emergency preparedness and sexual fixation.
jokes.explanation: Clever Dennis moment — he's using 'in our minds' to simultaneously justify going to the store and admit his real motivation is Jackie Denardo. The logic is entirely about the woman, dressed up as rationality. Character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I happened to be out in L.A. during the riots. I was on business.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: And to steal ski equipment, I guess.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I went in for a loaf of bread, I took some skis. Everybody's happy.

jokes.text: And they've left. They've left now. I'm only still here 'cause I'm not as quick as them.
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are discussing boarding up windows; the guys have all snuck out to go to the store while this was being arranged.
jokes.punchline: Dee does a dry address to camera acknowledging she's been abandoned, with the humiliating admission that she couldn't run fast enough to follow.
jokes.explanation: One of the cleaner mockumentary talking-head beats in the episode. The specific detail — she's still there not because she chose to stay, but because she's physically slower — is a funny and specific humiliation. The flat delivery implied by the phrasing makes it land. Also an efficient visual joke: the camera pans to an empty room while Dee explains.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: What's a hurricane party?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: A hurricane party's exactly what it sounds like. It's a party during a hurricane at our bar, Paddy's Pub.

jokes.text: Is that a pickled egg? / No. It's an egg I brought from home.
jokes.setup: Dee and Frank are left behind in the bar after everyone else has fled to the store.
jokes.punchline: Frank is eating an egg he insists is 'from home,' the distinction being entirely meaningless but delivered with defensive seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Tiny gem. The callback to pickled eggs works perfectly, and Frank's insistence that this is 'an egg I brought from home' as though that matters is very funny. It also implies he routinely carries a loose egg in his pocket. The economy is exceptional — the entire joke is nine words. High quotability because of its absurdist specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, he was probably down here with Mac, watching you rape girls and eating pickled eggs.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I don't rape girls, come on. Yeah, and I don't eat that many pickled eggs, but...

jokes.text: The gang arrives at the store and immediately spots Jackie Denardo in person — 'Oh, my God. Ooh-hoo-hoo. Aw! They're spectacular.'
jokes.setup: The gang went to the All American Home Center ostensibly to buy emergency supplies.
jokes.punchline: Their first action upon arriving is to immediately locate and rhapsodize over Jackie Denardo's body — ignoring all hurricane preparedness.
jokes.explanation: Payoff of the Jackie Denardo setup — the gang followed the news anchor to the location instead of actually preparing. Functional running gag execution, though the joke itself is fairly simple. The escalation of going to the STORE just to see her is the comedic element.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, we got a sweet bunker, too.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, well... It's, like, so secure, people can't get in or out if we don't want 'em to.

jokes.text: Imagine that image in 3-D.
jokes.setup: Mac sees Jackie Denardo in person for the first time.
jokes.punchline: His immediate thought is to mentally render her in 3-D — returning to Charlie's earlier 3-D TV proposal, now applied to real life.
jokes.explanation: Good callback execution — takes the earlier absurdist 3-D TV logic and applies it to seeing her live in person, as though real life is not 3-D enough. Economy is excellent. Brief but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: How did you not know... that the reason I invited you back to my bar... was to bang you? Get out of here! Get the hell out of here! Get... Get out of here! Shoo away from me!

jokes.text: For all we know, it could be the end of days.
jokes.setup: The gang debates whether to go to the Poconos or stock up on supplies.
jokes.punchline: Mac escalates to 'end of days' as a casual contingency, treating apocalypse-level framing as a reasonable planning consideration.
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing but not particularly original — 'end of days' as hurricane hyperbole is a fairly obvious beat. The character work isn't strong enough to elevate it above a functional transition moment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dude, they have amazing stuff here. I'm totally prepared. Check this out. How sweet is that?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You think girls are gonna want to come back to a bar with a man dressed the way you're dressed and carrying a hatchet?

jokes.text: Hey, you know what I was thinking? In addition to supplies, it might be nice to grab some girls... This Jackie Denardo chick... She's sparked another storm inside me, if you know what I mean.
jokes.setup: The gang is ostensibly planning emergency supply acquisition.
jokes.punchline: Mac pivots to 'grab some girls' as a supply item, with 'sparked another storm inside me' as a terrible pun he's clearly proud of.
jokes.explanation: The 'sparked another storm inside me' pun is the kind of terrible wordplay that fits Always Sunny's register — not clever enough to be a good pun, which makes it funny that Mac clearly thinks it's great. Functional but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah. They're gonna be, like, 'Look at this sweet dude, his awesome gear and his awesome hatchet. He's prepared, he's ready for anything. Storm coming? Hatchet coming.'

jokes.text: We could use 'em to repopulate the planet or something. That'll be great to have them.
jokes.setup: Mac suggests getting girls to ride out the storm with them.
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately frames women as reproductive resources for species continuation, with 'or something' making it even more sinister by suggesting it's not even his main motivation.
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — the casual eugenics framing is perfectly in character for his narcissistic worldview. 'Or something' and 'That'll be great to have them' are both funny qualifiers that make the horror feel offhand. Sets up the 'race of super giant-breasted women' escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's Cricket!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Cricket.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, what are you doing down here, Cricket?

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I come down the bunker sometimes when it rains.

jokes.text: I'd at least like to find one, like, Mexican or Mayan or something for predictions.
jokes.setup: Dee refuses to entertain the 'get girls' plan.
jokes.punchline: Charlie, still confused about Mayans vs. Mexicans, wants to find 'a Mayan or Mexican or something' for end-of-days prophecy consultancy.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Mayan/Mexican confusion. 'Or something' is a perfect Charlie qualifier — he's not even sure what he's looking for, just someone vaguely indigenous-adjacent. Consistent character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: No, I ain't going to no hospital. They euthanize the homeless. They're goddamned death camps!

jokes.text: No, but get some batteries though. You be the battery guy, and I'll be the... the 'chicks and tits' guy.
jokes.setup: Mac tries to redirect to practical supplies, then immediately assigns himself a role.
jokes.punchline: Mac designates himself 'the chicks and tits guy' as an official division of labor — a formal job title for objectification.
jokes.explanation: The job-title framing of 'chicks and tits guy' is the joke — it's a formal division of hurricane preparedness labor. Good economy; the pause before 'chicks and tits guy' as though he's figuring out the title sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We could dress him up and take him upstairs, and then the looters would think he's the owner of the bar, and they'd have their way with him, and if he died, you know, it's on them, and-and not on us.

jokes.text: Frank's media bias lesson: 'What do you think those people are doing — surviving or looting?' / 'They're surviving.' / 'Ah. Okay.' [Hurricane Katrina footage of white people] vs. 'What do you think these people are doing — looting or surviving?' / 'Well, they're looting.' / 'Ah, of course.' [Rodney King riots footage of Black people]
jokes.setup: Frank sets up an apparent media critique about racial bias in coverage of looting vs. survival.
jokes.punchline: Dee demonstrates exactly the bias Frank is describing by calling white people 'surviving' and Black people 'looting' without hesitation — the lesson is on her, not the media.
jokes.explanation: One of the more structurally sophisticated jokes in the episode. Frank appears to be making a progressive media criticism point, but the joke is that Dee demonstrates the bias herself — she's the subject of the lesson, not the audience. The parallel structure (ask same question twice, reverse racial context, observe Dee's different answer) is tightly constructed. Genuinely smart writing for Always Sunny.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: You're marching me to the ovens.

jokes.text: It's the media, see? When it's white people, it's survival. And when it's black people, it's looting. / No, Frank. It's because the white people are stealing bread and the black people are stealing speakers. If the white people were stealing stereo equipment, I would say they were looting too.
jokes.setup: Frank delivers his media bias thesis after Dee demonstrates the bias.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately undercuts Frank's correct observation with an object-based rationalization that is itself a form of racial stereotyping — she thinks she's being logical and fair.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest piece of writing. Dee's rebuttal to Frank's media bias point is itself an expression of a racial assumption — she has accepted that the Black people are specifically stealing speakers (a stereotype), which is the bias Frank was describing, and she doesn't see it. The 'if white people were stealing stereo equipment, I would say they were looting' self-satisfied addendum makes her think she's being consistent when she's already conceded the stereotype. It's a genuinely intelligent joke that also works as pure character comedy — Dee is always certain she's the most enlightened person in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Being of sound mind and body, do solemnly pledge that I do not have a boyfriend. Nor am I currently engaged in a sexual relationship with another individual, females excluded.

jokes.text: How do you know the blacks don't have bread in those speakers?
jokes.setup: Dee has explained that the difference between 'surviving' and 'looting' is based on what objects are being taken.
jokes.punchline: Frank offers an absurdist rebuke: maybe the speakers contain bread — which is both a genuinely absurd image and a reductio ad absurdum of Dee's object-based reasoning.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. It's nine words that completely detonate Dee's rationalization. The image of bread stored inside stolen speakers is absurd and funny on its own; as a logical response it also works ('you're judging necessity by object type, but objects can be used differently'). The economy is extraordinary — Frank accomplishes a philosophical argument and a surrealist image simultaneously. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I hereby agree to be easygoing, to engage in playful conversation, to always act as though I desire your penis even when I don't.

jokes.text: I happened to be out in L.A. during the riots. I was on business. And to steal ski equipment, I guess. / Yeah, well, I went in for a loaf of bread. I took some skis. Everybody's happy.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals he appears in riot footage — Dee asks what he was doing there.
jokes.punchline: Frank initially says 'business,' then immediately amends it to also include stealing ski equipment. His justification ('went in for bread, took skis, everybody's happy') is both a perfect character moment and an absurd non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: The 'I went in for a loaf of bread, I took some skis' is a great Frank line — it uses the classic 'went in for X, left with Y' shopping admission structure, but with maximally incompatible items. 'Everybody's happy' as a satisfied conclusion when it clearly isn't true for everyone is very Frank. The character integration is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I love it. Where do I sign?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Okay, again, um, you don't sign anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: If we're doing a contract, I want to sign it, so...

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This isn't a contract for you, Charlie.

jokes.text: Everybody's happy. / Not the people who own the skis.
jokes.setup: Frank has concluded that stealing skis during the L.A. riots was a mutually beneficial outcome.
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat correction that the ski owners are, in fact, not happy.
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man puncture of Frank's self-serving logic. Brief, economical, and functional. The joke is entirely in Dee's flat tone pointing out the obvious oversight. Not a great joke on its own but a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We would create a race of super giant-breasted women, you know? I'd start sleeping with your daughters, you'd sleep with my daughters, I'd sleep with your daughters' daughters, you'd sleep with my daughters' daughters. We die, our sons would sleep with our daughters' daughters' daughters.

jokes.text: Oh, shit! All right, calm... Oh, my God! The power went out! / Calm down. / This is terrible! We gotta get... Jesus! / That's why I like to have this little baby with me.
jokes.setup: The power goes out dramatically in the bar.
jokes.punchline: Frank responds to the power outage not with panic but with smug satisfaction — he has a flashlight (his 'little baby'), prepared as always in his trash bag and egg-pocket.
jokes.explanation: Functional scene-transition moment. Frank's calm competence in chaos is a character note, but the joke isn't particularly crafted. 'Little baby' as his term for a flashlight is mildly amusing. Mostly serves plot.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Have you gotten into the cheese?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: There's a whole cheese section. I went nuts.

jokes.text: Oh, no, I'm inviting them back to our very cool bar that we own. / Oh! Cool, cool. Yeah, we got a sweet bunker too. It's, like, so secure, people can't get in or out if we don't want 'em to.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis approach women at the store, trying to invite them to Paddy's Pub.
jokes.punchline: Dennis corrects Mac for mentioning the bunker, then Mac pivots to describing the bunker as a selling point but frames it as a lock-in facility where the occupants have no exit control — which sounds like a kidnapping scenario.
jokes.explanation: 'People can't get in or out if we don't want 'em to' is an accidentally terrifying sales pitch. Mac is trying to emphasize security but instead describes a prison. The women's visible discomfort (implied) makes this a good cringe moment. Very character-specific to Mac's obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: It's freezing outside. / You're gonna catch cold and then everyone's going to get sick in the bunker.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What are you talking about, freezing? It's sunny as shit.

jokes.text: You guys like pickled eggs? We got sardines too.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are attempting to charm attractive women into coming to their bar.
jokes.punchline: Charlie enters the pitch with pickled eggs and sardines as selling points — the worst possible snack appeal.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie moment. The pickled egg running gag peaks here with the worst possible timing — using it as a seduction pitch. 'We got sardines too' as a bonus offer makes it worse. The escalation from 'do you want to come to our cool bar' to 'pickled eggs and sardines' is a perfect comedic descent. Very high character integration — only Charlie would think these are selling points.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Don't make me do it, Cricket, I will slice you in half.

jokes.text: Yeah, we got a bunch of other, you know, normal food and normal stuff there too.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just offered pickled eggs and sardines to the women they're trying to impress.
jokes.punchline: Mac scrambles to reassure the women that they also have 'normal food and normal stuff' — which is both accurate and an admission that the previous items are abnormal.
jokes.explanation: Decent damage-control beat. The word 'normal' repeated twice as Mac tries to establish baseline normalcy is a good character moment — his awareness that Charlie's pitch was bad is itself funny. Functional cringe beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: For the good of the race? / So come to the bar and, uh, oh, and I have a contr-- an agreement, and I need you to sign...

dialogue.speaker: News Crew
dialogue.line: Storm's not going to hit Philly. It's just going to drizzle.

jokes.text: Sure. We don't want just the two of you. You got to bring your girlfriends. That's a requirement.
jokes.setup: The women have agreed to come and said to bring their friends.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis enthusiastically demand more women as a 'requirement' — framing women as inventory items they're ordering.
jokes.explanation: 'That's a requirement' is the right word choice — it frames women as supply-chain items. Decent character beat but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Jackie
dialogue.line: How am I supposed to turn that into news?

dialogue.speaker: Producer
dialogue.line: I don't know, find some other way to make these people go nuts. We need a story.

jokes.text: How did you not know that the reason I invited you back to my bar was to bang you? / Get outta here. / Get the hell outta here! Get... Get outta here! Shoo away from me!
jokes.setup: The women reveal they have boyfriends and ask if they can bring them.
jokes.punchline: Dennis, humiliated, turns his rejection into righteous indignation — not apologizing but shooing the women away as though they were the problem, complete with 'Shoo away from me!'
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dennis moments in the episode. The inversion is perfect: he was trying to pick them up, they declined, so he treats THEM as the offenders and shoos them away like pigeons. 'Shoo away from me!' is a remarkable phrase — it implies they were the ones pursuing him. 'That was too dark. They lied to me.' (his subsequent line) further reveals his totally warped sense of social reality. Extremely character-specific and highly quotable.

dialogue.line: Maybe we can turn this into global warming. That always gets people whipped up, huh?

jokes.text: That was too dark. They lied to me.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have just been rejected and Mac watched Dennis yell 'shoo away from me' at two women.
jokes.punchline: Mac's summary: they 'lied to him' — as though the women had made a promise to have sex with them and broken it.
jokes.explanation: Very economical character beat. 'They lied to me' is the kind of complete reality distortion that defines these characters — the women never implied they'd have sex with Mac, but he's framing their existence as a promise they failed to keep. 'Too dark' is funny too: acknowledging Dennis went too far, but not in a self-aware way.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: You're gonna treat me like a dog, huh? You're gonna treat Cricket like a dog?

jokes.text: If you want to entice these ladies, you gotta talk about the bunker. You got to lead with the bunker. / No. You end with the bunker. Or you don't talk about the bunker at all.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are debriefing their failed pickup attempt.
jokes.punchline: They disagree about bunker disclosure strategy — 'lead with the bunker' vs. 'end with the bunker' — treating a doomsday shelter as a romantic asset that requires strategic reveal timing.
jokes.explanation: Excellent exchange. The assumption underlying both positions — that the bunker is a seduction tool rather than a horror — is perfectly delusional. Dennis's 'you end with the bunker' as a romantic reveal strategy (like a magician saving the best trick) vs. 'or you don't talk about the bunker at all' covering both bases is very well-structured. The debate treats the bunker as equivalent to 'do you reveal your beach house on the first date or third?' Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.line: We can only accept cash at this time.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, shit.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.line: Okay, well, you got cash?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I only have cards.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Charlie, where's the cash I gave you?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Mac took off with all our cash! He just took off!

jokes.text: Are you kidding me? You think girls are gonna want to come back to a bar with a man dressed the way you're dressed and carrying a hatchet? / Yeah. They're gonna be like, 'Look at this sweet dude. His awesome gear and his awesome hatchet. He's prepared. He's ready for anything. Storm coming? Hatchet coming.'
jokes.setup: Mac is in full disaster gear with a hatchet, suggesting this will attract women.
jokes.punchline: Mac provides an internal monologue of how he imagines women will react, which is entirely about his own power fantasy — 'Storm coming? Hatchet coming' is his imagined tagline.
jokes.explanation: 'Storm coming? Hatchet coming' as Mac's self-imagined catchphrase is very good — it makes no sense as a seduction line but sounds exactly like what Mac would think is incredibly cool. The cadence of 'sweet dude / awesome gear / awesome hatchet / prepared / ready for anything' is a perfect imitation of Mac's internal hype voice.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Loot, loot, time to loot, loot! Loot, loot! Take everything! Kill the machines! It's their fault! Kill the machines...!

jokes.text: What was that? Was that a rat? / It was a looter. What... / Behind us.
jokes.setup: Dee and Frank are navigating the dark bar after the power outage.
jokes.punchline: Frank's instant assumption that any noise is a 'looter' rather than something mundane like a rat.
jokes.explanation: Transitional scene beat. Frank's paranoia is consistent with his character, and 'Behind us' as a dramatic utterance about what turns out to be Cricket is a decent setup for the Cricket reveal. Functional but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's the end of days, it's the end of days! Pandemonium has struck. Come to the bunker, come to the bunker!

jokes.text: Oh, a looter! Shoot him! / No, don't shoot! / It's Cricket!
jokes.setup: Frank has heard something in the dark bunker and assumes it's a looter.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately yells 'Shoot him!' — escalating from 'it might be a looter' to 'execute them' instantly, before the reveal that it's Cricket.
jokes.explanation: Frank's escalation from suspicion to 'Shoot him!' is very on-brand. The Cricket reveal lands well because Cricket appearing in the worst possible context is a running show-level gag. Solid scene beat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dennis, I got her, Dennis, I got her!

jokes.text: Aah! I come down to the bunker sometimes when it rains.
jokes.setup: Cricket is discovered wounded in the dark bunker — everyone initially assumes he's a looter.
jokes.punchline: Cricket's explanation is that he casually uses their bunker as his shelter when it rains — he's so destitute that a storage closet is his weather refuge.
jokes.explanation: Very sad and very funny. The casual 'sometimes when it rains' implies this is a routine thing — Cricket has incorporated the gang's bunker into his regular homeless shelter rotation. The audience understands the full arc of Cricket's degradation that makes this land. High character integration for Cricket.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: 3-D boobies. Now, this is news.

jokes.text: They euthanize the homeless. They're goddamned death camps!
jokes.setup: Frank insists they take Cricket to the hospital because he's been shot.
jokes.punchline: Cricket refuses to go to the hospital because he believes hospitals euthanize homeless people — calling them 'death camps.'
jokes.explanation: 'Goddamned death camps' is a great escalation. The paranoia is funny and also, given Cricket's total degradation, almost understandable. The grandiosity of 'death camps' applied to a Philadelphia hospital is excellent. Very Cricket.

jokes.text: I have a hand, Frank. It's a little... I have a hole in it. Big deal.
jokes.setup: Frank points out that Cricket has a hole in his hand (from being shot).
jokes.punchline: Cricket minimizes a gunshot wound as 'a hole in it, big deal' — either because he's delirious or because his baseline of suffering is so high that a gunshot barely registers.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Cricket line. 'I have a hole in it. Big deal.' is a perfect expression of Cricket's absolute floor of suffering — he's been through so much worse (canonically) that a gunshot hole in his hand is barely noteworthy. The correction 'I have a hand, Frank' before the admission 'it has a hole in it' is structurally perfect. Extremely character-integrated and highly quotable.

jokes.text: We could dress him up and take him upstairs. Then the looters would think he's the owner of the bar, and they'd have their way with him, and if he died, you know, it's on them and not on us.
jokes.setup: Cricket is bleeding and needs hospital care. The gang is debating logistics.
jokes.punchline: Mac's proposed solution is to use Cricket as a looter-decoy/sacrificial body — dressing him as the bar owner so looters will kill him instead of them, and if he dies from his existing wound, that's the looters' legal problem.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly horrible suggestion delivered with complete earnestness. The 'it's on them and not on us' legal reasoning is very Always Sunny — the gang's primary concern is always liability rather than morality. Frank's immediate 'That's good. Let's just do that' is the button that makes it land as a full joke.

jokes.text: You're marching me to the ovens!
jokes.setup: Frank overrules everyone and insists they take Cricket to the hospital.
jokes.punchline: Cricket, being dragged to the hospital, cries out 'You're marching me to the ovens!' — a Holocaust reference expressing his conviction that the hospital will kill him.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the 'death camps' line, escalated to 'marching me to the ovens.' The hyperbole is extreme enough to be very funny — Cricket comparing a hospital trip to genocide. Highly quotable and an excellent button for the Cricket scene. The escalation from 'death camps' to full Holocaust imagery is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: The contract Dennis has written for women to sign: 'I hereby agree to be easygoing, to engage in playful conversation, to always act as though I desire your penis even when I don't.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been working on 'an agreement' for the women at the bar.
jokes.punchline: The agreement is revealed to be a consent/behavior contract Dennis has written for women to sign, with a clause that they must 'always act as though I desire your penis even when I don't' — a deeply disturbing document delivered as a totally normal business arrangement.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dennis moments and one of the episode's high points. The contract is a perfect expression of Dennis's complete disconnect from normal social reality — the idea that you need a legally binding document ensuring women perform attraction 'even when they don't' is both horrifying and completely in character. 'State your name' / 'Charlie Kelly' / 'No, their name' is a great setup. The legal language applied to romantic/sexual expectations is a classic Dennis bit. The 'sort of goes on and on like that for a while' implies this is a lengthy document. This is Dennis Reynolds as a character: the manipulation codified into paperwork.

jokes.text: I love it. Where do I sign? / Again, um, you don't sign anywhere. / If we're doing a contract, I want to sign it, so... / This isn't a contract for you, Charlie.
jokes.setup: Dennis explains the contents of the women's contract to Charlie.
jokes.punchline: Charlie enthusiastically wants to sign the contract himself — missing entirely that it's for the women, and Dennis has to repeatedly clarify this.
jokes.explanation: Very Charlie — he's so enthusiastic about the contract's contents that he wants to be bound by it himself, completely misunderstanding the transaction. 'If we're doing a contract, I want to sign it' is both very Charlie (he loves official documents) and completely baffling. Dennis's confused repeated clarifications are great.

jokes.text: If we're doing a contract, I want to sign it. / This isn't a contract for you, Charlie. / It's not?
jokes.setup: Dennis clarifies Charlie shouldn't sign the agreement
jokes.punchline: Charlie's genuine surprise and mild disappointment that the contract isn't for him — suggesting he wanted this formalized agreement for his own reasons
jokes.explanation: A continuation of the Charlie-signs-the-contract bit. His 'it's not?' is a small but good beat — genuine confusion about why he wouldn't be a party to this document. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Charlie, I might be in love with this woman. Not for the right reasons, mind you.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie have spotted Jackie Denardo in person.
jokes.punchline: Dennis admits possible love and immediately disclaims that the reasons are wrong — the acknowledgment that there ARE 'right reasons' for love, and these are definitely not them, is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Dennis line. 'Not for the right reasons, mind you' is an incredible qualifier — Dennis has enough self-awareness to know his reasons are wrong but zero interest in having the right reasons instead. The 'mind you' is a lovely formal touch that makes the admission sound like a legal disclaimer. Very quotable and very Dennis. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: We would create a race of super giant-breasted women, you know? I'd start sleeping with your daughters. You'd sleep with my daughters. I'd sleep with your daughters' daughters. You'd sleep with my daughters' daughters. We die, our sons would sleep with our daughters' daughters' daughters. It's like a perfect society.
jokes.setup: Dennis has decided Jackie Denardo is the perfect woman to 'start over the new world with.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis lays out a multi-generational selective breeding program focused on breast size, involving cross-sleeping with each other's daughters and granddaughters — which is a eugenics program wrapped in an incest framework, presented as utopian planning.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely escalating and deeply disturbing in the best Always Sunny way. The escalation from 'daughters' to 'daughters' daughters' to 'daughters' daughters' daughters' has a hypnotic, cumulative horror. 'It's like a perfect society' as the concluding thesis — delivered with evident satisfaction — is a perfect button. The logic is internally consistent, which makes it worse. High originality: not a standard dark joke, more of a full monologue with an arc. Charlie's 'it could get a little messy' as understatement is a great reaction.

jokes.text: I see where you're going with that, but it sounds like it could get a little messy.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just described a multi-generational incestuous eugenics breeding program.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's only objection is that it 'could get a little messy' — a profound understatement for what Dennis has described, suggesting Charlie follows the logic fine but has logistical concerns.
jokes.explanation: 'Could get a little messy' as the only reservation about an incest-eugenics program is a perfect understatement. Charlie's acceptance of the basic premise (he 'sees where Dennis is going') makes it funnier — he has no moral objection, just project management concerns. Very economical reaction beat.

jokes.text: Let's work out a new agreement, you know. All right, we'll come up with a separate agreement. Who sleeps with whose daughter?
jokes.setup: Charlie has flagged that the daughter-sleeping plan 'could get messy.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately proposes a new contract — a separate legal agreement governing who sleeps with whose descendants — treating this as a standard business document.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the Dennis contract motif — his response to any social complexity is to draw up a document. The specificity of 'who sleeps with whose daughter' as a contract clause is very funny. Character integration is excellent.

jokes.text: I feel very, very nervous. I don't usually get nervous. / You want me to help you out? Yeah. No. / I'll go over there with you. / No, no, no. I want you to stay as far away from me as possible. You're standing too close to me as it is actually.
jokes.setup: Dennis wants to approach Jackie Denardo but is thrown by genuine attraction.
jokes.punchline: Dennis, who fancies himself an expert seducer, admits to being nervous — then refuses Charlie's help while simultaneously being too embarrassed to have Charlie witness him. The 'you're standing too close' rebuff implies Charlie's proximity is itself shameful.
jokes.explanation: Good character vulnerability beat — seeing Dennis flustered is effective because it's rare. The 'I don't usually get nervous' self-aware admission is classic Dennis. The 'you're standing too close' as an additional insult to Charlie is a good extra beat.

jokes.text: Have you gotten into the cheese? There's a whole cheese section. / I bet there is. I went nuts.
jokes.setup: Dennis notices Charlie smells bad and asks if he's been into the cheese section.
jokes.punchline: Charlie confirms immediately: 'I went nuts' — the casual confession that he ate an enormous amount of store cheese while everyone was busy is very Charlie.
jokes.explanation: 'I went nuts' as a matter-of-fact confession is perfect Charlie. The implication that he ate enough cheese to smell noticeably is funny. Good economy — 'I bet there is. I went nuts.' is four words of pure Charlie character.

jokes.text: You guys, I don't mean to be a bother, but are we almost at the hospital?
jokes.setup: Cricket has been shot and is bleeding in the car while Frank drives erratically.
jokes.punchline: Cricket's polite, apologetic inquiry — 'I don't mean to be a bother' — from someone bleeding to death in the back seat is a profound and very funny understatement of his situation.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Cricket line. The politeness — 'I don't mean to be a bother' — from someone in a life-threatening situation is a masterful understatement. It also reflects Cricket's total social marginalization: even bleeding out, he's apologetic about inconveniencing people. 'Are we almost at the hospital?' as a child-in-the-car-trip question makes it funnier. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Shut the hell up, Cricket! Okay? I'm driving as fast as I can! Do you not see that?
jokes.setup: Cricket politely asks if they're almost at the hospital while bleeding.
jokes.punchline: Frank responds with maximum irritation to a dying man's gentle inquiry — treating it as nagging.
jokes.explanation: Frank's irritability at a dying man is consistent character work. The gap between Cricket's excessive politeness and Frank's excessive annoyance is the joke. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: What are you doing, Frank? / I'm getting air. / You're sucking it all up with your panicking. It's freezing outside. / What are you talking about? Freezing? It's sunny as shit.
jokes.setup: Frank opens the car window while driving Cricket to the hospital in a storm.
jokes.punchline: Frank accuses Dee of 'sucking up all the air' with her panicking; Dee says it's freezing; Frank claims it's 'sunny as shit' — both completely ignoring the hurricane that supposedly prompted all of this.
jokes.explanation: 'Sunny as shit' — Frank's casual dismissal of the weather everyone's been panicking about — is a good thematic irony beat. The storm being apparently non-existent even as they respond to it in chaos is the episode's core joke. 'You're sucking it all up with your panicking' is a funny Frank construction.

jokes.text: Mac went to the Poconos, left them stranded by the All American with the supplies! / With the supplies? No! No, no, no, no! I'm not getting stranded in the bunker with no supplies!
jokes.setup: Frank learns that Mac has taken the car and apparently fled to the Poconos.
jokes.punchline: Frank's instant priority is not stranding the people (Charlie and Dennis) but stranding the SUPPLIES — his primary concern is the resource, not the humans.
jokes.explanation: Frank's panic is about the supplies, not about Charlie and Dennis being stranded — his friends are secondary to his supply-hoarding concerns. Good character moment that shows Frank's survivalist priorities.

jokes.text: You guys, what about me? I'm in pain. I'm in... / Shut up! / Goddamn you, Cricket! Goddamn you! It's not about you!
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are panicking about supplies while Cricket is bleeding in the back seat.
jokes.punchline: Cricket tries to remind them he's in pain; Frank explodes at him, saying 'It's not about you!' — to a gunshot victim in a car being driven to his hospital.
jokes.explanation: 'Goddamn you, Cricket! It's not about you!' to a gunshot victim actively being driven to the hospital is a great line. Frank's rage at Cricket for existing in a conversation about Frank's supply problem is very consistent with how the gang always treats Cricket. High character integration.

jokes.text: I don't wanna die. / Don't make me do it, Cricket. I will slice you in half!
jokes.setup: Cricket expresses fear of dying; Frank is trying to drive.
jokes.punchline: Frank's response to Cricket saying he doesn't want to die is to threaten to slice him in half — a threat to kill him in response to his fear of death.
jokes.explanation: 'I will slice you in half' in response to 'I don't want to die' is a very good piece of dark comedy — Frank's solution to Cricket's death anxiety is to threaten a worse death. The timing has to be right, but the construction is sharp. Very Frank.

jokes.text: Dennis awkwardly introduces himself to Jackie Denardo: 'I'm Dennis... Reynolds.' 'Hi.' 'Hi... Dennis.' 'I have a bar. I own a bar. It's my bar.'
jokes.setup: Dennis, who normally oozes self-confidence and considers himself irresistible, is trying to approach Jackie Denardo.
jokes.punchline: Dennis falls apart completely — the triple redundancy ('I have a bar. I own a bar. It's my bar.') and the staggered name introduction reveal total incompetence in the face of genuine attraction.
jokes.explanation: 'I have a bar. I own a bar. It's my bar.' is a perfect comedic tricolon — each repetition adds no new information but reveals increasing desperation. The character subversion is excellent: Dennis's whole identity is as a master seducer, and here he's completely falling apart. Very character-integrated because it shows the gap between his self-image and reality. The staggered name exchange ('I'm Dennis... Reynolds' / 'Hi. / Hi... Dennis.') is also very well-paced cringe.

jokes.text: And, you know, for the good of the race?
jokes.setup: Dennis is rambling through his pitch to Jackie Denardo, losing coherence.
jokes.punchline: Dennis invokes 'the good of the race' as a seduction argument — an accidental eugenics pitch delivered to a woman he just met.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the 'race of super giant-breasted women' scheme — now leaked into Dennis's actual pitch to Jackie as a reason she should come to his bar. The fact that he's clearly delivering his actual plan while thinking it sounds like a reasonable pickup line is very funny. Economy excellent.

jokes.text: Oh, and I have a contra... an agreement. Excuse me, sir. Yeah, it's about the storm. Okay? Storm's not gonna hit Philly. It's just gonna drizzle.
jokes.setup: Dennis is mid-pitch to Jackie Denardo, about to show her the contract.
jokes.punchline: He's interrupted by a weather official who nonchalantly reveals the storm has been downgraded to a light drizzle — completely undermining every event in the episode.
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the episode's central premise — the entire crisis was media hype, the storm isn't coming, Frank was right all along. The casual delivery ('It's just gonna drizzle') after everything that's happened is perfect understatement. This is a great structural joke even if the line itself isn't exceptional.

jokes.text: How am I supposed to turn that into news? / I don't know. Find some other way to make these people go nuts. We need a story.
jokes.setup: Jackie Denardo is informed the storm isn't coming.
jokes.punchline: The weather official's casual instruction to 'find some other way to make these people go nuts' — explicitly articulating that the news's job is to manufacture panic rather than report facts.
jokes.explanation: The media satire lands here: the person responsible for weather news explicitly says 'make people go nuts' as a job description. It validates Frank's conspiracy theory from the opening and gives the episode thematic coherence. 'We need a story' is the capsule version.

jokes.text: Hey, Todd. Storm's just been downgraded. Apparently we're just gonna get a light drizzle. / Goddamn it! I have a bunker.
jokes.setup: Jackie learns the storm is downgraded and passes this along casually.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response to 'storm downgraded to drizzle' is not relief but 'Goddamn it! I have a bunker' — his fury is about the now-useless bunker he was using as a seduction prop.
jokes.explanation: 'Goddamn it! I have a bunker.' is a great line — Dennis is furious that the storm being downgraded makes his primary seduction asset worthless. It's the perfect expression of his skewed priorities. The bunker was never about survival; it was always about impressing women. Highly quotable and a good callback to the bunker-strategy debate.

jokes.text: If you get in the bunker with me, then you'll be totally safe. For the good of the race, we can create an entire... Oh, my God! Get lost, creep!
jokes.setup: Dennis pivots from the downgraded storm to pitching the bunker and repopulation plan to Jackie Denardo directly
jokes.punchline: Jackie Denardo's immediate and emphatic rejection: 'Get lost, creep!'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Dennis's entire Jackie Denardo obsession — after all the planning and contracts and breeding programs, her actual response to him is 'get lost, creep.' The gap between his self-image and reality is the whole Dennis Reynolds joke, and this lands it cleanly. The escalation from his elaborate pitch to her two-word dismissal is structurally very good.

jokes.text: Maybe we can turn this into global warming. That always gets people whipped up, huh?
jokes.setup: Jackie's producer suggests they need a new story now that the storm is downgraded.
jokes.punchline: Dennis, in the background, starts free-associating news angles — suggesting 'global warming' as a crowd-panic topic — inadvertently becoming a news producer despite not being one.
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny scene beat — Dennis accidentally contributing to the news-panic machine. The media satire is a bit on-the-nose here compared to the subtler version earlier. Not a highlight.

jokes.text: You're gonna treat me like a dog, huh? / You're gonna treat Cricket like a dog?
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been rejected and called a creep by Jackie Denardo.
jokes.punchline: In his humiliated muttering, Dennis says 'treat me like a dog' — which is immediately picked up by Cricket, who has been literally treated like a dog throughout the series, implying Cricket takes the dog-treatment question personally.
jokes.explanation: Very good meta-joke. Dennis uses 'like a dog' as a hyperbolic expression of humiliation; Cricket, who has canonical dog-related degradation in the show's history, hears it and takes it personally/literally. The juxtaposition of Dennis's wounded pride with Cricket's actual suffering is sharp. High character integration for both.

jokes.text: If you get in the bunker with me, then you'll be totally safe. For the good of the race, we can create an entire... / Oh, my God! Get lost, creep!
jokes.setup: Dennis has been pitching Jackie Denardo on coming to his bunker for 'the good of the race.'
jokes.punchline: Jackie Denardo, the professional news anchor Dennis has been obsessing over all episode, calls him a creep and dismisses him — the ultimate deflation of his fantasy.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Dennis/Jackie arc — his elaborate plan results in being called a creep. The gap between his self-image and reality is the whole Dennis joke, and 'Get lost, creep!' is an appropriately direct delivery of that reality. Good structural payoff.

jokes.text: Hey, you look kind of Mayan. You wouldn't happen to be a Mayan, would you?
jokes.setup: Charlie has been wandering the hospital looking for a Mayan.
jokes.punchline: Charlie approaches a random person and asks if they're Mayan based on their appearance — the culmination of his entire Mayan prophecy obsession from the episode.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff for the Mayan running gag. The directness of 'You look kind of Mayan' as a physical identification method (using no actual visual information a non-Mayan person could use) is very funny. Charlie's total commitment to finding a Mayan prophet is a great character thread.

jokes.text: I think I found a Mayan. / We've been looking all over for you. / Cricket's out in the car bleeding like a pig. Seriously?
jokes.setup: Frank finds Charlie in the hospital.
jokes.punchline: Frank's update that Cricket is 'bleeding like a pig' out in the car is delivered as a quick aside — Cricket's medical emergency is secondary to finding Charlie.
jokes.explanation: Transitional dark beat. Cricket's continuing suffering mentioned as an afterthought is consistent with how the show treats him. Frank's 'seriously?' reaction to Charlie's Mayan claim is a good reaction beat. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Folks, listen up! I'm sorry, but our credit card machines just went down due to a system overload. We can only accept cash at this time. / Shit! / Okay, well, you got cash? / I only have cards. / Charlie, where's the cash I gave you? / Mac took off with all our cash! He just took off!
jokes.setup: The gang has filled a cart with supplies but has no cash — Dee had the cash, which Mac apparently took when he fled to the Poconos.
jokes.punchline: The credit card machines going down is Dee's robopocalypse prediction come true — society collapsing because of machine failure — delivered at the worst possible moment.
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff — Dee's entire Y2K machine-fear subplot is validated when the credit card machines fail at the critical moment. Mac taking the cash is also a nice unseen escalation. The gang's immediate helplessness validates everything Dee said in the bunker.

jokes.text: Hey, folks! Folks, listen up! I'm sorry, but our credit card machines just went down due to a system overload. We can only accept cash at this time.
jokes.setup: Dee's earlier 'robopocalypse' prediction that machine failure would collapse society
jokes.punchline: The credit card machines go down — validating Dee's theory exactly — at the worst possible moment for the gang who gave the cash to Mac
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural payoff — Dee was right, and the episode rewards the callback. The timing (Mac has the cash, they only have cards) means the machine failure cascades into full chaos. Good payoff to a planted setup.

jokes.text: I told you! I told you! I told you we're dependent on machines. You guys, once the machines go down, then society collapses! We're going to hell in a handcart.
jokes.setup: The credit card machines have gone down and the gang can't pay for their supplies.
jokes.punchline: Dee's vindicated robopocalypse speech — 'I told you!' — finally delivered as correct, though the situation she described as world-ending is really just a hardware problem at a Home Depot.
jokes.explanation: The 'I told you' vindication beat is satisfying structurally. 'We're going to hell in a handcart' as her summary is a funny old-fashioned expression applied to a credit card machine failure. Good callback payoff.

jokes.text: I got a plan, okay? Let's just start looting shit. Let's just grab shit. / Yes! / No, you can't loot until the crowd whips up into a frenzy. / The crowd is whipped up into a frenzy. They just stole my cart! / I-I think the time will be evident. / Well, what are we waiting for? / I don't know.
jokes.setup: The gang can't pay for their supplies and needs a new plan.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate plan is looting; Dennis says you need to wait for the crowd to reach a frenzy first; the crowd is already stealing things; Dennis still isn't sure the moment is right; Frank doesn't know when to start.
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier exchanges in the episode. Dennis's insistence on looting best practices ('you can't loot until the crowd whips up into a frenzy') while the crowd is already rioting around him is a great piece of absurdist character work. His inability to identify the obvious frenzy-moment despite being surrounded by it is perfect Dennis pomposity. 'I don't know' as Frank's honest final answer is a great button.

jokes.text: Loot! Loot! Time to loot! Loot! Loot! Loot! Take everything... and anything! Kill the machines! It's their fault! Kill the machines before they kill us!
jokes.setup: The gang is debating when it's the right moment to start looting.
jokes.punchline: Dee, the designated 'reasonable' character, is the one who incites the riot — screaming 'Kill the machines!' while looting, fulfilling her robopocalypse obsession in the most chaotic way possible.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character payoff. Dee has been the voice of reason all episode, but she's the one who starts the riot while screaming about machines — her Y2K paranoia and opportunistic looting instincts converging in one glorious moment. 'Kill the machines before they kill us!' is a great line that ties together the looting subplot and the machine-dependency theme. High earned comedy because it's been set up carefully.

jokes.text: Just seconds ago, a car crashed through the building, and the crowd is scattering. Despite the fact that the storm has been downgraded, the people have worked themselves into an uncontrollable frenzy!
jokes.setup: Frank has apparently driven the car through the front of the store; chaos has erupted.
jokes.punchline: Jackie Denardo is now reporting on the riot as breaking news — the gang's panicked incompetence has inadvertently created the news story she needed after the storm downgrade.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural payoff. The gang's looting has become the very news spectacle that Jackie needed after the storm was downgraded. 'Despite the fact that the storm has been downgraded' is the key phrase — the media hysteria they were worried about has been self-created. This ties the episode's themes together: media hype, looting panic, and the gang's self-destruction converge perfectly.

jokes.text: It's the end of days! This is the end of days! Pandemonium has struck! Come to the bunker! Come to the bunker!
jokes.setup: The store is in chaos — a car has crashed through, there's a riot, Jackie Denardo is broadcasting live.
jokes.punchline: Mac is screaming 'It's the end of days!' — his earlier casual escalation is now sincere — while Dennis reverts to 'Come to the bunker!' as his only offer to anyone.
jokes.explanation: Good chaotic climax with callback elements. Dennis reverting to 'Come to the bunker!' in a genuine catastrophe — still using it as a pickup line in the middle of a riot — is consistent and funny. Mac's 'end of days' callback landing as literally true (they've created their own apocalypse) is a satisfying irony.

jokes.text: Dennis, I got her! Dennis, I got her!
jokes.setup: Chaos has erupted in the store; everyone is running.
jokes.punchline: Charlie has apparently physically grabbed Jackie Denardo (or someone) in the chaos — 'I got her!' implying he's captured rather than wooed her — his version of helping Dennis.
jokes.explanation: Very quick but effective — Charlie's attempt to help Dennis with Jackie Denardo involves physically acquiring her rather than charming her. The word 'got' rather than 'found' or 'talked to' implies capture. Brief but character-perfect.

jokes.text: Is this the hospital?
jokes.setup: Frank has driven the car into the All American Home Center in the chaos; Cricket is in the back seat.
jokes.punchline: Cricket, still focused entirely on getting medical care for his gunshot wound, emerges from the crashed car asking if this is the hospital — his needs are so basic and so ignored that he genuinely doesn't know what's happening.
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly. Cricket, who has been a bleeding afterthought in a car since scene one of his appearance, emerges from a car-crash into a burning Home Depot during a riot and asks if it's the hospital. The gap between his simple need (medical care) and the absolute chaos around him is total. The delivery has to be completely flat — which it clearly is — and that makes it devastating and funny. One of the episode's best single lines. Near-maximum economy.

jokes.text: 3-D boobies.
jokes.setup: Total chaos. Frank has driven through the wall. Jackie Denardo is there broadcasting. Everything is on fire.
jokes.punchline: Mac's only comment, apparently looking at the in-person Jackie Denardo in the chaos, is '3-D boobies' — the callback to Charlie's opening 3-D TV proposal, now delivered as Mac's sincere observation that he is seeing boobies in 3-D for the first time.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Two words that pay off two separate setups — Charlie's 3-D TV proposal in the opening scene and Mac's 'Imagine that image in 3-D' at the store. In the middle of maximum chaos (car through the wall, riot, fire, Jackie broadcasting live), Mac's singular reaction is the quiet, satisfied observation that he is finally seeing boobies in 3-D. The economy is perfect — the entire callback works in two words. The fact that it comes RIGHT after Cricket's 'Is this the hospital?' makes the juxtaposition even richer: one man needs emergency medical care; the other is experiencing a dream come true. Landmark Always Sunny button.

jokes.text: Now this is news.
jokes.setup: Jackie Denardo needed a story after the storm was downgraded. The gang has inadvertently created a full riot.
jokes.punchline: 'Now this is news' — Jackie's satisfied professional conclusion that the chaos the gang created is exactly the story she needed.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button for the episode's media satire theme. 'Now this is news' closes the loop on Jackie's 'we need a story' request and validates Frank's opening media-hype theory. Four words that do a lot of work. Great economy.

jokes.text: Now this is news.
jokes.setup: Jackie Denardo wanted a story; the gang has inadvertently created one
jokes.punchline: 'Now this is news' — Jackie's professional satisfaction at the riot she partly caused, closing the media satire loop
jokes.explanation: Four words that close the entire media satire arc. Jackie Denardo, who manufactured hurricane fear and then immediately needed a new story when downgraded, is now thrilled by the chaos the fear-mongering produced. 'Now this is news' is delivered with professional satisfaction — she has no self-awareness about her role in creating it. Excellent economy and a perfect thematic button. Comparable in function to the best sitcom act-out lines.

tmdb_overview: As a hurricane threatens Philadelphia, Mac, Dennis and Charlie go to a mall to buy supplies and check out the large breasted TV reporter broadcasting from there, while Frank and Dee prepare Paddy's, and its basement bunker, for the storm.
